questions.stem: A 78-year-old man presented with dehiscence of his sternal wound with associated drainage of purulent material. He had undergone a 3-vessel CABG 3 weeks earlier after an episode of STEMI and abnormal cardiac catheterization that was not amenable to stenting. On examination, his temperature was 100.2°F (37.8°C), his heart rate was 99 beats/minute, his blood pressure was 100/70 mmHg, and his respiratory rate was 20 breaths/ minute. Investigations: CT chest: retrosternal fluid collection with associated stranding and cortical erosion in the sternal bone Blood cultures: negative
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Aspiration of fluid via interventional radiology with culture and targeted antibiotics
Bedside debridement with surface culture and targeted antibiotics
Surgical intervention for wash out, operating room culture sampling, and targeted antibiotics
Wound care without need for antibiotics given negative blood cultures

questions.explanation: Surgical intervention for wash out, operating room culture sampling, and targeted antibiotics This patient is presenting with post-CABG mediastinitis, with evidence of sternal osteomyelitis and involvement of hardware. In this case, the best strategy to control the source and have better chance of treatment success is with OR revision, wash out, removal of hardware, and debridement of bone. OR cultures would be most definitive to identify the organism and target antimicrobial therapy. The duration of therapy will vary depending on organisms, extent of infection, and response. The patient has purulent discharge and evidence of infected fluid in the deep tissue planes/bone, which would need source control and antimicrobial therapy for proper wound healing to occur in the surface. Wound care alone would be insufficient. Bedside debridement would only be superficial and surface cultures may not accurately represent the organisms causing deep tissue infection. Although aspirate may be useful for culture and organism identification, it will have limited ability to perform source control given the presence of hardware and infected bone that require debridement.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 4 Q17

questions.question: Woman with AVR (aortic valve replacement); 3 weeks later, sternal wound red, infected and patient febrile. Surgeon opens it up, debrides, packs wound. Cultures from wound and blood + S. aureus. Pt on Cloxacillin. Pt still febrile, wound still looks bad.

parts.text: List 2 sources for her ongoing fever
How would you treat this patient (give abx, mode of admin, frequency and duration)

cohort_answer.text: Sources of fever: MRSA (resistant to clox), mediastinitis/mediastinal abscess persisting, prosthetic valve IE. Tests: susceptibility testing on S. aureus isolate, CT chest to rule out mediastinitis/abscess, TEE. Treatment: Vancomycin based on weight and Cr until susceptibilities available; for mediastinitis, surgical debridement plus antibiotics (vancomycin if MRSA, cloxacillin if MSSA, increase frequency to q4h/consider continuous infusion); duration 2-3 weeks after sternal resection and pectoral flap, or 4-6 weeks if residual rib/sternal bone infection risk
